content: Seborrhoeic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that primarily affects the scalp, face, chest, and intertriginous areas. It is characterized by scaling and redness of the skin. Current treatment options include antifungal agents, anti-inflammatory agents, keratolytic agents, and phototherapy. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of topical pharmacological treatments with established anti-inflammatory properties for seborrhoeic dermatitis in adolescents and adults. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases up to September 2013, including the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, and the GREAT database. They also reviewed trial registries and reference lists of included studies to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The study included RCTs involving adolescents and adults (aged 16 years or older) diagnosed with seborrhoeic dermatitis of the scalp or face. The trials compared topical anti-inflammatory treatments, such as steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and lithium salts, with other treatments. Data collection and analysis were performed independently by pairs of authors, who assessed study eligibility, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Meta-analyses were conducted when feasible. A total of 36 RCTs involving 2706 participants were included in the analysis. Of these, 31 trials investigated topical steroids, seven examined calcineurin inhibitors, and three evaluated lithium salts. The comparative interventions included placebo, azoles, calcipotriol, a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory compound, and zinc, as well as comparisons between different anti-inflammatory treatments. The primary outcomes of interest were total clearance of symptoms, erythema, scaling, pruritus scores, and adverse effects. The risk of bias in the studies was frequently classified as unclear due to insufficient reporting of methods. Topical steroids were found to be more effective than placebo in achieving total clearance of symptoms in short-term trials (lasting four weeks or less) and in one long-term trial (lasting 12 weeks). Steroids also demonstrated greater efficacy in reducing erythema, scaling, and pruritus compared to placebo. Adverse effects were similar between the steroid and placebo groups. When comparing steroids to calcineurin inhibitors, there was no significant difference in total clearance in the short term. Both treatments were comparable in other efficacy outcomes, but adverse events were less common in the steroid group. Steroids and azoles showed similar rates of total clearance and adverse effects in the short term, but steroids were more effective in reducing erythema and scaling. Mild (class I and II) and strong (class III and IV) steroids were comparable in terms of efficacy and adverse events, except for long-term total clearance, which was more frequently achieved with mild steroids. Calcineurin inhibitors were more effective than placebo in reducing erythema and scaling in one study, but there was no difference in total clearance or adverse events in the short term. In another study, calcineurin inhibitors were comparable to azoles in terms of erythema, scaling, and adverse effects during longer-term treatment. Lithium salts were more effective than placebo in achieving total clearance, with a comparable safety profile. Compared to azoles, lithium salts were more effective in achieving total clearance in short-term treatment. The authors concluded that topical steroids are an effective treatment for seborrhoeic dermatitis of the face and scalp in adolescents and adults. There was no significant difference between mild and strong steroids in the short term. There is some evidence supporting the use of topical calcineurin inhibitors or lithium salts. Azoles appear to be as effective as steroids in achieving short-term total clearance, but steroids were more effective in other outcomes. Calcineurin inhibitors and azoles were found to be comparable, while lithium salts were more effective than azoles in achieving total clearance. Steroids were similarly effective to calcineurin inhibitors but had fewer adverse effects. Most of the included studies were small and of short duration, typically lasting four weeks or less. The authors recommend that future trials should be appropriately blinded, include larger sample sizes (more than 200 to 300 participants), and compare steroids to calcineurin inhibitors or lithium salts, as well as calcineurin inhibitors to azoles or lithium salts. Follow-up periods should be at least one year, and quality of life should be assessed. Additionally, there is a need for the development of well-validated outcome measures.
